text: Last lesson was about generating images. This lesson is about the other direction — models that understand images. A vision-language model isn't a text model with an image plugin bolted on; it's one model, trained so images and text share the same reasoning space. That's why it can read a chart, not just describe a picture.

Here's a real request to Claude's Messages API with an image. It looks exactly like the message shape from Chapter 3, with one new content block type: image, carrying a source object. That source can be base64 data embedded directly, a URL to a hosted image, or a file_id from a one-time upload — useful when the same image gets reused across turns in a conversation.

Three limits that actually matter once you're building something real. How many images per request — up to a few hundred depending on the model, but only twenty on claude.ai itself. Which formats are supported — JPEG, PNG, GIF, WebP, with animations read as just their first frame. And resolution drives cost: Claude breaks an image into 28 by 28 pixel patches, and every patch is a billable visual token, the same way every word is a billable text token.

A screenshot at 1920 by 1080 costs somewhere around one-thousand-five-hundred to twenty-seven-hundred visual tokens, depending on the model's resolution tier. That's not trivia — if your app sends a full-resolution screenshot on every single turn of a long conversation, that cost adds up exactly the way unbounded text history does.

Per the documented limitations, straight from the provider: accuracy drops on low-quality, rotated, or very small images. Counting objects in an image is approximate, not exact. Coordinate and spatial output is approximate, not pixel-perfect. And no current vision-language model can reliably tell you whether an image itself was AI-generated. Verify before you rely on any of it.

One model, reasoning over images and text together, with real costs and real documented blind spots. Next lesson moves past pictures entirely — audio and speech models, and what it actually takes to build something that listens or talks back.
